newsitem.title: Czech republic: FOCUS - Czech PM greets opposition split on budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Czech PM greets opposition split on budget.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, facing a cliffhanger vote on the 1997 state budget, praised a leading Social Democrat on Wednesday amid signs that an opposition split could hand the government victory.

Klaus said that Social Democrat Jozef Wagner, who chairs the parliamentary budget committee, was putting the interests of the nation first by recommending that deputies approve the draft in its first reading, expected later on Wednesday.
Klaus's centre-right coalition, which lost its majority in the house in June elections, has hinted it might resign if the opposition succeeded in forcing changes to the balanced budget.
Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman, political enemy of Klaus, has demanded changes to the draft to curtail government authority over the budget once approved by parliament.

The Social Democrats (CSSD) at various times have also demanded a slowing in liberalisation of heating prices and state rents, a crackdown on tax evasion and economic crime, and more subsidies for the needy once prices are liberalised.
It is not yet clear how far the CSSD will push their demands, or if the party will vote in unison.
In a speech to parliament on Tuesday night, Wagner was highly critical of the the government but ended with a recommendation to pass the budget.

Klaus, welcoming signs of an opposition split, said on Wednesday: "I have expressed my disagreement with what Mr. Wagner said but I also want to appreciate Mr Wagner for suggesting...that the budget should go to a second reading.
With Senate elections due next month, the political climate is heating up. Klaus has repeatedly accused the centre-left Social Democrats of trying to reverse post-communist reforms.
The three-party coalition holds 99 out of 200 seats in parliament and therefore only needs a couple of opposition defections to win the budget vote.
Pavel Ledvinka a member of the junior coalition party, the pro-business Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA), gave only qualified support to the draft budget.

"The ODA accepts the budget as a member of the coalition with many objections because it diverges from the profile of the government which we participated in. We will support it in the first reading," he told the budget debate.
Earlier, the ODA's parliamentary leader Ivan Masek said the budget did not go far enough in cutting taxes and woule not be anti-inflationary because it was balanced and did not run a surplus.
Frictions within the three-party coalition have often come into the open, notably since it lost its parliamentary majority in elections earlier this year.

Klaus has not explicitly made the vote a confidence issue. If the government loses, it must resubmit the budget with changes demanded by the opposition. The three party coaltion has so-far rejected having to submit to any opposition demands.

To win, the CSSD must vote as a bloc with the two other oppposition parties, the little-reformed Communists and the far-right Republicans. Both extremist parties have told parliament they would reject the government draft.
